What Types of Eye Injuries Could Occur in a Car Crash?

Car crash eye injuries can occur in numerous ways. The airbag could hit you in the face or eyes when it deploys. If you are in the front seat, you could strike the dashboard or other hard surfaces inside the vehicle. Some people who sustain eye injuries may get hit by flying debris caused by the crash, such as shattered glass, pieces of metal or plastic, objects in the car or something else. In some cases, an airbag may deploy improperly, causing your eyes to be exposed to hazardous chemicals. Eye injuries that are commonly occur in a car wreck include:

Black Eye

Direct trauma to your eyes or the area around your eyes could cause your eyes to bleed, leading to tissue discoloration and a black eye. One way this could happen, for example, is if you hit the side of the door or steering wheel during the impact.. A black eye is not necessarily serious, but it is not easy to tell if other damage may have occurred, such as a torn retinae. In some cases, victims may develop "raccoon eyes" which simply means you have two black eyes.  This distinction is important, however, because it could be an indication of a brain injury.

Lacerations

Flying glass from a shattered window or windshield during a car crash could cut your eyelids. Serious eyelid lacerations can cause underlying damage to your eyeball, socket, retina or another part of the eye.

Orbital Fractures

It usually takes excessive force to break or fracture the bones in your eye socket. For example, if you hit your eye on the steering wheel due to the impact of a car crash. Orbital fractures are sometimes associated with serious brain or eye injuries that can affect coordination or even cognitive abilities.

Globe Ruptures

Blunt trauma or penetration of an eye can damage the cornea or sclera, the outermost layers of the eye. For example, the quick combustion of an airbag (less than a second) could mean a forceful impact on your face and, potentially, your eye.

Hyphema

When blood enters your eye’s anterior chamber, it becomes visible on your eyeball. A hyphema is typically caused by trauma to your eye and requires immediate medical attention to avoid permanent vision loss.

Chemical Burns

If your eye becomes exposed to any leaking chemicals from the vehicle after a car crash, you could suffer a chemical burn to your cornea or stem cells, leading to irritation or even blindness.

Traumatic Cataracts

Trauma to the eye could cloud your lens, causing blurred vision. Traumatic cataracts can gradually develop in the eye over time, so it is important to seek immediate medical attention if you experience any changes in your vision after a crash.

Retinal Detachment

The retina is the light-sensitive layer of tissue located in the back of your eye. A blow to your head during a car crash could rip the retina from the blood vessels in your eye. If you suffer from retinal detachment, your eyes may feel heavy, and you may see flashes or floaters. Retinal tears or a retinal detachment is an immediate emergency. Do not delay going to the ER as it could result in permanent vision loss.

Vitreous Hemorrhage

The vitreous humor is the gel between your retina and eye lens. Blunt trauma to your eye can cause hemorrhaging (bleeding) into the vitreous humor. Severe bleeding can be extremely dangerous if left untreated, potentially causing blindness.

Optic Nerve Damage

A blow to the eye during a car crash can put enough pressure on your optic nerve to bleed, cut off circulation and possibly cause permanent blindness.

Traumatic Brain Injuries (TBIs)

A TBI is caused by violent shock or impact to the head. This could result in different types of visual impairment, such as:
  • Blurry vision
  • Double vision
  • Loss of eye coordination
  • Light sensitivity
  • Visual memory loss

Symptoms of Eye Damage

If you suffered an eye injury from a car crash, you may experience some of the following symptoms:
  • Itchy eyes
  • Flashes of light
  • Swelling around your eye
  • Dark spots when you blink
  • Blood in or around your eyes
  • Blurry vision when you try to focus on an object
  • Reduced eye coordination or movement when you try to look up, down or peripherally

Treatment Option for a Car Crash Eye Injury

There are various options for treating an eye injury. The treatment you receive will depend on how serious your injury is:
  • Medication: A doctor might prescribe a drug to help clear an infection in your eye or manage pain and inflammation.
  • Eye patch: An eye patch can protect your eye while it heals after your injury.
  • Eye drops or ointments: If your eye is inflamed or dry, eye drops and ointments may lubricate it, reduce inflammation or prevent infection.
  • Rehabilitation: Prescription glasses, cryotherapy (therapy using cold temperatures), magnification devices, filters, etc. are types of rehabilitation designed to help victims regain visual function after a severe eye injury.
  • Surgery: Some injuries require surgery to repair damage to the eye, such as with a retinal tear, or to remove foreign objects.

Including Eye Injuries in a Georgia Auto Accident Claim

Georgia is an at-fault state. This means the driver at fault must pay for the other driver's injuries and damages through their insurance company. You can seek compensation for treatment of eye injuries and any other injuries from the crash. This includes the cost of:
  • Trips to the emergency room
  • Therapy related to your eye injury
  • Surgery
  • Prescription medication
  • Follow-up visits with doctors
For some crash victims, their eye injuries are severe enough to impact their emotional and mental health. Others may be unable to go to work or participate in activities or hobbies they once enjoyed. In this situation, you may be able to seek additional compensation for those damages. It is important to seek help from an experienced lawyer after a car crash. In Savannah, the experienced attorneys at Roden Law know how to evaluate victims’ damages to determine the full value of a claim. We also have the resources and experience managing car crash cases to gather strong evidence that supports your claim. You should not count on the insurance company to take care of you after suffering a serious car crash injury. They will be looking for some way to undercut your claim and lessen its value. Our trusted law firm knows how to effectively counter these tactics to protect the full value of your claim.

Table of Contents
  • Why Savannah's Intersections Are So Dangerous
  • The Most Dangerous Intersections in Savannah
  • Savannah's Most Dangerous Road Corridors
  • Common Causes of Intersection Crashes in Savannah
  • Georgia Traffic Laws That Protect You
  • What to Do After an Intersection Accident in Savannah
  • Proving Fault at a Dangerous Intersection
  • How a Savannah Car Accident Lawyer Can Help

Savannah is one of Georgia's most beautiful cities — but its roads tell a different story. With a mix of high-speed suburban corridors, aging infrastructure, and traffic volumes that have outpaced road design, certain Savannah intersections see a disproportionate number of serious and fatal crashes every year. According to the Georgia Department of Transportation, Chatham County consistently ranks among the top five Georgia counties for total traffic collisions, and the most dangerous time for intersection crashes in Savannah falls between noon and 6:00 PM. If you or a loved one has been injured at one of these dangerous intersections, understanding your legal rights under Georgia law — and the legal concept of negligence — is the first step toward obtaining fair compensation.

Why Savannah's Intersections Are So Dangerous

Several factors combine to make Savannah's intersections more hazardous than those in comparably sized cities. The city's rapid suburban growth — particularly along the Abercorn Street and DeRenne Avenue corridors — has pushed traffic volumes well beyond what these roads were originally designed to handle. Many Savannah intersections lack protected left-turn signals, dedicated turn lanes, or modern traffic control systems. The result is a dangerous mix of high-speed traffic, limited visibility, and driver confusion that produces hundreds of crashes each year.

Tourism adds another layer of risk. Savannah attracts more than 14 million visitors annually, many of whom are unfamiliar with local roads. Tourists distracted by GPS navigation, unfamiliar lane configurations, and the city's unique one-way street patterns contribute to a significant share of intersection collisions, particularly in the Midtown and Southside corridors.

Additionally, Savannah's flat coastal terrain and frequent afternoon rainstorms create dangerous conditions. Standing water at intersections reduces tire traction and visibility, and hydroplaning is a common contributing factor in rear-end and broadside crashes at Savannah's busiest crossroads.

The Most Dangerous Intersections in Savannah

Based on crash data compiled by the Georgia Department of Transportation and local law enforcement, these Savannah intersections consistently produce the highest number of collisions, injuries, and fatalities.

1. Abercorn Street and White Bluff Road

This intersection has earned the unwanted distinction of being Savannah's single most dangerous crossroads. It consistently leads the city in total crashes and produces more injury-related hospital transports than any other intersection in Chatham County. The convergence of heavy commercial traffic from Oglethorpe Mall, residential traffic from the White Bluff corridor, and vehicles entering and exiting nearby shopping centers creates constant conflict points. Rear-end collisions and T-bone crashes are especially common here during the afternoon rush between 4:00 and 6:00 PM. If you have been hurt in a crash at this intersection, a Savannah car accident lawyer can help you investigate whether the at-fault driver ran a red light, was distracted, or failed to yield.

2. Interstate 16 and Chatham Parkway

The I-16/Chatham Parkway interchange is one of Savannah's most feared stretches of road. Locals have nicknamed I-16 the "Devil's Highway" because of its history of high-speed fatal collisions, and the Chatham Parkway interchange sees more than 25,000 vehicles daily. The combination of highway-speed merging traffic, short ramp distances, and vehicles abruptly braking to navigate the interchange creates extremely dangerous conditions. Truck traffic is heavy along this corridor, as I-16 serves as Savannah's primary freight route connecting the Port of Savannah to Interstate 95 and points west. Truck accidents at this interchange frequently involve catastrophic injuries due to the speed differential between commercial vehicles and passenger cars.

3. King George Boulevard and Abercorn Street

This Southside intersection consistently ranks in the top three for accident frequency in Savannah. The six-lane Abercorn Street corridor meets the heavily trafficked King George Boulevard near several big-box retail centers, and the resulting traffic congestion produces a high rate of angle collisions and sideswipe crashes. Drivers attempting left turns across multiple lanes of oncoming traffic face particularly dangerous conditions, and pedestrians crossing Abercorn near this intersection are at elevated risk due to the wide roadway and limited crosswalk infrastructure.

4. Abercorn Street and Rio Road

The Abercorn/Rio Road intersection, located in one of Savannah's most commercially dense areas, produces a high volume of crashes driven by constant traffic entering and exiting retail parking lots, the proximity of multiple signalized and unsignalized access points, and aggressive driving by motorists frustrated with congestion. Distracted driving — particularly drivers looking at storefronts or phone navigation — is a significant factor at this intersection.

5. DeRenne Avenue and Truman Parkway

DeRenne Avenue serves as Savannah's primary east-west artery through Midtown, and its intersection with the Truman Parkway handles enormous traffic volumes as commuters travel between the residential Eastside and the commercial Southside. The narrow lanes on DeRenne, combined with frequent sudden stops and aggressive lane changes, make this intersection a hotspot for rear-end collisions. The proximity of Memorial Health University Medical Center increases pedestrian traffic in this area, creating additional hazards. Victims of crashes here may suffer traumatic brain injuries or spinal cord injuries that require extensive medical treatment.

6. Ogeechee Road and Chatham Parkway

This West Savannah intersection becomes especially hazardous during peak commuting hours. Ogeechee Road carries significant industrial and commercial traffic, including heavy trucks serving the port and warehouse districts. The intersection's geometry forces drivers into complex turning movements, and limited sight distances at certain approach angles increase the risk of broadside collisions. Motorcycle riders are particularly vulnerable at this intersection because other drivers frequently fail to check for smaller vehicles before turning.

7. Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard and 37th Street

Located near the border between Savannah's historic district and Midtown, this intersection sees a mix of local residential traffic, tourist traffic, and commercial vehicles. The relatively narrow lanes, on-street parking, and pedestrian activity in this area create conditions where distracted or speeding drivers are especially dangerous. Pedestrian accidents are a serious concern at this intersection, particularly during evening hours when visibility is reduced.

8. Abercorn Street and Victory Drive (US-80)

The meeting of two of Savannah's busiest thoroughfares creates a particularly complex intersection. Victory Drive carries high-speed traffic between Savannah's islands and the city's interior, and Abercorn brings heavy north-south commercial traffic. The multiple turn lanes and signal phases at this intersection confuse unfamiliar drivers, and the high speed of approaching traffic means that crashes here tend to produce severe injuries. Wrongful death cases arising from crashes at this intersection are not uncommon.

Savannah's Most Dangerous Road Corridors

Beyond individual intersections, several Savannah road corridors stand out for their overall crash frequency.

Abercorn Street (Full Corridor)

Abercorn Street is Savannah's most dangerous road, period. Stretching from the Historic District through Midtown and deep into the Southside suburbs, Abercorn handles enormous traffic volumes and is lined with commercial development that generates constant turning movements and driveway conflicts. Multiple intersections along Abercorn rank among the city's most dangerous, and the corridor as a whole produces more crashes per mile than any other road in Chatham County.

DeRenne Avenue

DeRenne Avenue is notorious for its narrow lanes, heavy congestion, and aggressive driving. As the primary east-west route through Midtown Savannah, DeRenne handles commuter traffic that regularly exceeds the road's design capacity. Sudden stops, aggressive lane changes, and the clustering of medical facilities near Memorial Health create a constant stream of hazards for drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians. The 4:00 PM to 6:00 PM rush hour window is particularly dangerous along this corridor.

Interstate 16

I-16 between Savannah and the I-95 interchange carries heavy freight and commuter traffic and has a well-documented history of fatal crashes. The highway's design — including short merge zones and limited shoulders in certain sections — contributes to high-speed rear-end and sideswipe collisions. Trucks account for a disproportionate share of I-16 crashes, and the injuries from these collisions are often catastrophic. If a truck driver's negligence caused your crash on I-16, you may have claims against both the driver and the trucking company.

Common Causes of Intersection Crashes in Savannah

Understanding what causes intersection crashes helps accident victims identify the at-fault party and build a strong injury claim. The most common causes of intersection crashes in Savannah include:

  • Red light running: Drivers who enter an intersection after the light has turned red cause some of the most violent T-bone collisions. Georgia law under O.C.G.A. § 40-6-20 requires drivers to obey all traffic control devices.
  • Failure to yield on left turns: Left-turn accidents are among the most common intersection crash types in Savannah. Drivers who misjudge the speed of oncoming traffic or attempt to turn during a yellow light frequently cause broadside collisions.
  • Distracted driving: Cell phone use, GPS navigation, and passenger distractions cause drivers to miss red lights, stop signs, and the movements of other vehicles in intersections.
  • Speeding: Excessive speed reduces a driver's ability to stop at intersections and dramatically increases the severity of injuries in a crash. Georgia's speed limits are governed by O.C.G.A. § 40-6-181.
  • Impaired driving: Drunk and drugged driving remains a leading cause of fatal intersection crashes in Savannah, particularly during late-night and early-morning hours.
  • Poor road design: Some of Savannah's most dangerous intersections lack adequate turn lanes, sight lines, signage, or signal timing. When a government entity's failure to maintain or properly design a road contributes to a crash, the injured party may have a claim against the responsible agency under Georgia's governmental immunity exceptions.

Georgia Traffic Laws That Protect You

Georgia has specific traffic laws that govern driver behavior at intersections and provide a legal framework for holding negligent drivers accountable after a crash.

Statute of limitations: Under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33, you have two years from the date of your accident to file a personal injury lawsuit in Georgia. Missing this deadline typically means losing your right to compensation entirely. South Carolina allows three years under S.C. Code § 15-3-530.

Comparative fault: Georgia follows a modified comparative fault rule under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33. You can recover compensation as long as you are less than 50% at fault for the accident, but your award is reduced by your percentage of fault. For example, if you suffered $100,000 in damages but were found 20% at fault, your recovery would be $80,000. South Carolina applies a similar rule with a slightly higher threshold — you can recover if you are less than 51% at fault.

Right-of-way rules: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-70 through § 40-6-76 establish right-of-way rules at intersections, including requirements to yield to traffic already in the intersection, obey traffic signals, and yield to pedestrians in crosswalks. Violations of these statutes can serve as strong evidence of negligence in your injury claim.

Hit and run: Under O.C.G.A. § 40-6-270, leaving the scene of an accident that causes injury or death is a felony in Georgia. If a hit-and-run driver injured you at a Savannah intersection, your car accident attorney can work with law enforcement and use surveillance footage, witness statements, and other evidence to identify the responsible driver.

What to Do After an Intersection Accident in Savannah

The steps you take immediately after an intersection crash in Savannah can significantly affect your ability to recover full compensation. Here is what you should do:

  1. Call 911 and request medical attention. Georgia law requires you to report any accident that causes injury, death, or significant property damage. The police report generated from this call becomes critical evidence in your claim.
  2. Seek medical treatment immediately. Even if you feel fine at the scene, many serious injuries — including traumatic brain injuries and soft tissue injuries — may not produce symptoms until hours or days later. Prompt medical documentation creates a direct link between the crash and your injuries.

A fully loaded tractor-trailer traveling at highway speed can weigh 80,000 pounds, and the force of a collision between a commercial truck and a passenger vehicle at 65+ mph frequently produces traumatic brain injuries, spinal cord injuries, and fatalities. If a truck driver's fatigue, distraction, or impairment caused your crash on I-16, you may have claims against both the driver and the trucking company.

Interstate 95 Through Chatham County

Interstate 95 is the most heavily traveled north-south highway on the East Coast, and it runs directly through the Savannah metropolitan area. Federal crash data bears that out: across 2022–2024, I-95 recorded more fatal crashes than any US interstate except I-10 — 924 fatal crashes and 1,020 deaths nationally, second of 222 interstate designations (NHTSA Fatality Analysis Reporting System, annual files, accessed 25 August 2026). The Chatham County segment carries a mix of long-distance travelers, local commuters, and heavy commercial truck traffic that generates a high volume of serious crashes.

Why I-95 is so dangerous near Savannah:

  • Speed and volume: Vehicles traveling at 70+ mph in dense traffic leave little margin for error. A momentary distraction at highway speed can result in a catastrophic crash.
  • Truck concentration: I-95 carries enormous volumes of freight traffic, and the clustering of trucks creates dangerous conditions for passenger vehicles, especially in construction zones and near interchange areas.
  • The I-95/I-16 interchange: This junction is a known bottleneck where merging traffic patterns produce frequent rear-end and sideswipe collisions.
  • Weather: Savannah's coastal climate produces sudden rain squalls that reduce visibility and create hydroplaning conditions on I-95's high-speed lanes.

Victims of I-95 crashes often face complex legal situations involving out-of-state trucking companies, multiple insurance carriers, and commercial vehicle regulations. An experienced Savannah car accident lawyer can navigate these complexities and ensure you pursue all available sources of compensation.

Abercorn Street: Savannah's Deadliest Road

Abercorn Street is the most dangerous road in the City of Savannah. Stretching from the Historic District south through Midtown and deep into the Southside suburbs, Abercorn carries enormous traffic volumes through a corridor lined with commercial development that generates constant turning movements, driveway conflicts, and parking lot access points.

Why Abercorn Street is so dangerous:

  • Commercial density: The Southside segment of Abercorn is lined with shopping centers, restaurants, and big-box retailers. Vehicles are constantly entering, exiting, and crossing Abercorn to access these businesses, creating an unending stream of conflict points.
  • High-crash intersections: Multiple Abercorn intersections rank among the city's most dangerous, including Abercorn at White Bluff Road, King George Boulevard, Rio Road, and Victory Drive (US-80).
  • Pedestrian danger: The wide, multi-lane roadway and the concentration of commercial destinations put pedestrians at significant risk, particularly near Oglethorpe Mall and the Abercorn/DeRenne intersection.
  • Speed transitions: Abercorn's character changes dramatically from a slow-moving historic district street to a high-speed suburban arterial, and the speed transitions catch drivers — especially tourists — off guard.

DeRenne Avenue: Narrow Lanes, Heavy Congestion

DeRenne Avenue is Savannah's primary east-west artery through the Midtown area, and it is notorious among local drivers for its dangerous conditions. The road carries traffic volumes that far exceed its design capacity, and the resulting congestion creates a pressure-cooker environment where aggressive driving and crashes are common.

Key danger factors:

  • Narrow lanes: DeRenne's lane widths are substandard by modern engineering criteria, giving drivers less room to maneuver and increasing the severity of sideswipe crashes.
  • Medical facility traffic: The proximity of Memorial Health University Medical Center to the DeRenne corridor generates heavy traffic including ambulances, medical transport vehicles, and visitors unfamiliar with the area.
  • Rush hour intensity: The 4:00 PM to 6:00 PM evening commute is DeRenne Avenue's most dangerous window. Sudden stops and aggressive lane changes during heavy congestion produce a high rate of rear-end collisions.
  • The DeRenne/Truman Parkway intersection: This intersection handles massive volumes as commuters travel between Savannah's Eastside and Southside neighborhoods, and it consistently ranks among the city's top crash locations.

I-516 (Lynes Parkway): High-Speed Danger

I-516, also known as Lynes Parkway, connects downtown Savannah to I-16 and the Southside. Despite being a relatively short highway, I-516 has a disproportionate history of serious crashes driven by high travel speeds, limited shoulders, and the merging patterns at its interchanges. Speeding is endemic on I-516, and the crashes that result from excessive speed tend to be severe. Motorcycle riders are especially vulnerable on I-516, where the high speed of surrounding traffic and limited visibility on the highway's curves create deadly conditions.

Common Causes of Highway Crashes in Savannah

  • Speeding: Excessive speed reduces stopping distance and dramatically increases crash severity. Georgia speed limits are governed by O.C.G.A. § 40-6-181, and the Georgia Super Speeder law (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189.1) imposes additional penalties for drivers convicted of traveling 75+ mph on two-lane roads or 85+ mph on any road.
  • Truck driver fatigue: Federal hours-of-service regulations limit how long commercial truck drivers can operate without rest, but violations are common. Fatigued truck drivers on I-16 and I-95 pose an extreme danger to everyone sharing the road.
  • Distracted driving: Cell phone use, GPS navigation, and in-vehicle infotainment systems divert driver attention at highway speeds, where a few seconds of distraction can cover the length of a football field.
  • Impaired driving: Alcohol and drug impairment remains a leading cause of fatal highway crashes in Chatham County.
  • Tailgating: Following too closely on congested highways like I-16 and Abercorn Street eliminates the stopping distance needed to avoid rear-end collisions when traffic slows suddenly.

What to Do After a Highway Crash in Savannah

  1. Move to safety if possible. Highway crashes create extreme secondary collision risks. If your vehicle is drivable, move it to the shoulder. Turn on hazard lights and stay behind the guardrail.
  2. Call 911 immediately. Georgia law requires reporting accidents involving injuries. Highway crashes often require specialized response including fire rescue and traffic control.
  3. Seek medical treatment even if you think your injuries are minor. Adrenaline can mask pain from serious injuries like concussions, internal bleeding, and soft tissue damage.
  4. Document the scene with photographs if it is safe to do so. Capture vehicle positions, road conditions, weather, skid marks, and any debris patterns.
  5. Do not discuss fault with other drivers or insurance representatives at the scene.
  6. Contact a Savannah car accident lawyer before providing recorded statements to any insurance company.

East Bay Street is dangerous for pedestrians because it is a four-lane arterial carrying fast through-traffic directly alongside one of the most walked corridors in Savannah. On one side you have Emmet Park's oaks and the steps down toward River Street; on the other, a steady stream of drivers who are watching for the Historic District's one-way circulation instead of the person stepping off the curb. That mismatch — arterial speed next to constant foot traffic — is exactly where people get hit.

The eastern Historic District stacks several hazards into a few blocks:

  • The square grid. Drivers circle Washington Square, Greene Square, Warren Square, Crawford Square, and Columbia Square while tourists step off curbs mid-block, watching the scenery instead of traffic.
  • The Truman Parkway hand-off. Harry Truman Parkway ramps meet East President Street at the eastern edge of downtown, dumping 55 mph commuter traffic into pedestrian-dense blocks with almost no speed transition.
  • The bar corridor after dark. Late-night impaired driving along East Bay Street is a recurring factor in nighttime crashes near the riverfront.

  • Event surges. St. Patrick's Day, riverfront festivals, and SCAD event weekends flood the squares and East Bay Street with unfamiliar drivers on the one-way grid.

Eric Roden, Roden Law's founding partner, points out that the most winnable Historic District pedestrian cases often turn on the small physical details of the corridor — a faded crosswalk line, a blocked sightline behind a trolley, a rideshare stopped where it never should have been — which is why documenting the exact spot on East Bay Street where you were hit matters as much as the police report itself.

Georgia Crosswalk Law and Who Has the Right of Way

In a marked crosswalk, the driver almost always owes you the duty to stop. Right of way is not automatic everywhere, though. Mid-block, outside a marked crosswalk, pedestrians generally must yield to vehicles — which is why so many tourist crashes around Washington Square and Columbia Square become fault disputes. That does not mean you lose. It means the facts of the specific crossing decide the case, and a careful review of the scene, the signals, and witness accounts often shifts fault back onto the driver who was speeding or not paying attention. You generally have two years from the date of injury to file a pedestrian injury lawsuit in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). Miss that window and the court will almost certainly throw the case out, no matter how badly you were hurt. Two years feels like plenty of time until months disappear into surgeries, physical therapy, and insurance calls — so the deadline is a reason to talk to a lawyer early, not later.

That is a fraction of the standard limitations period, and getting the notice wrong can bar the claim entirely.

Being partly at fault does not end your claim in Georgia. The state follows modified comparative negligence: you can still recover damages as long as you are less than 50% at fault, though your award is reduced by your own percentage of fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). If you were 20% responsible and your damages are $100,000, you recover $80,000.

This rule matters for East Bay Street crashes, because insurers reflexively blame the pedestrian — "you crossed mid-block," "you were on your phone," "you'd been drinking." Even if some of that is true, it does not automatically bar you. Pushing your share of fault below the line is where a lawyer earns the recovery, and our Savannah car accident lawyers handle the striking-vehicle side in tandem.

If the driver who hit you took off, you may still have a clear path to compensation. Leaving the scene of an injury crash is a crime under Georgia's hit-and-run law (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-270), and when the driver is never identified, your own uninsured motorist (UM) coverage often becomes the primary source of recovery (O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11). Many people do not realize their auto policy's UM coverage can pay even when they were on foot, not behind the wheel.

Late-night hit-and-runs cluster on East Broad Street and Wheaton Street, where the bar traffic thins out and drivers gamble that no one saw them. We cover this scenario in depth for walkers in our page on hit-and-run pedestrian accidents, and the UM-coverage mechanics in our overview of hit-and-run accident claims. When impaired driving is the cause, our resource on drunk-driver pedestrian accidents explains the added avenues — including potential dram-shop exposure — that can widen your recovery.

What to Do After You're Hit on East Bay Street

The single most important step is to get medical care immediately, even if you feel "okay." Adrenaline masks serious injuries, and a gap in treatment is the first thing an insurer uses against you. Memorial Health University Medical Center — the region's Level I trauma center — is roughly ten minutes away via the Truman Parkway.

Then, if you are physically able:

  1. Call 911 and make sure a Savannah-Chatham police report is created.
  2. Photograph everything — the crosswalk, skid marks, the vehicle, the intersection, and where you landed relative to the curb.
  3. Get names and numbers from tourists and bystanders before they scatter; on East Bay Street, most witnesses are visitors who leave town.
  4. Do not give a recorded statement to the driver's insurer before speaking with a lawyer.
  5. Save your shoes and clothing exactly as they are — they can corroborate the point of impact.
